passage: Aadhya was waiting outside the staff room again, notebook hugged to her chest, when Professor Yash came out with his tea. "Sir, I copied your lecture line by line. Should I do a master's in soil science? Whatever you say, I'll do it." The college sat at the edge of a small town, and the peon was already watching them with a smile. "Sir, I can carry your files to the lab," she added. Yash felt the warmth of it, and the weight. "Carry your own," he said gently. "I can tell you how I made my choice, but I have never worked outside a university. For placements, ask the cell downstairs. And you decide, then tell me why." She looked a little deflated, then took out her pen anyway.

qa.q: What did Aadhya offer to carry to the lab?
qa.a: She offered to carry his files to the lab.

qa.q: What might Yash be feeling when Aadhya says she will do whatever he says?
qa.a: He feels warmed by her trust but weighed down by it, which is why he hands the decision back and asks for her reasons.

qa.q: How could Yash keep guiding her without making her lean on him?
qa.a: He can keep asking for her reasons and point her to the placement cell and others who know more than he does, so her own judgement grows. 🙂

qa.q: How might Aadhya see his refusal to let her carry the files?
qa.a: She is a little deflated at first, perhaps fearing he is pulling away, but taking out her pen shows she still values his help.

grounding: A student hangs on the professor's words and he guides her without dependence while stating his limits.

passage: My name is Vijay, and for three weeks I crossed the corridor to avoid Professor Sarita's room. Everyone said she failed people for fun. My thermodynamics assignment was half done and I could not understand the second question, yet my stomach turned every time I saw her door. Finally I wrote down three specific doubts, read the chapter again, and went during office hours with sweaty palms. She looked up, said "Sit," and asked me to show my working. I expected a scolding. Instead she circled one line and said, "Good start, wrong sign here." Ten minutes. I walked out lighter, almost laughing. She still scares me a little, but now I know she forgets her glasses on her forehead.

qa.q: How many specific doubts did Vijay write down before going?
qa.a: He wrote down three specific doubts.

qa.q: Why did Vijay's stomach turn every time he saw her door?
qa.a: He was scared of her strictness, having heard she failed people, and feared a scolding about his half done assignment.

qa.q: What would you advise Vijay to do if he gets stuck again?
qa.a: Go early to office hours again with specific doubts and his own working, instead of avoiding her until the problem grows.

qa.q: How might Professor Sarita see a student turning up at office hours?
qa.a: She probably sees a student who wants to learn; her calm "Sit" and quick correction suggest she is glad to help, not eager to scold.

grounding: A student afraid of a strict professor prepares, attends office hours and finds her more approachable.

passage:
"You've been quiet since the lab meeting. What happened?" Amandeep asked, dropping her bag on the hostel bed.
"Dr. Mehta gave the conference slot to Tanmay. His results are weaker. Everyone knows his cousin plays cricket with Dr. Mehta."
"Maybe there's a reason."
"Maybe. But my poster wasn't even mentioned. I used to copy how Dr. Mehta wrote problem statements. I thought everything about that was perfect."
"So are you going to tear up your notebook?"
"I almost did." Chandrika opened it and looked at the first page. "But the way of framing a question still works. That part is mine now, fair or not."
"And the slot?"
"I'll ask plainly why. And I won't decide that every professor is the same."

qa.q: Who got the conference slot?
qa.a: Tanmay got the conference slot.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's remark about copying the problem statements suggest about how she felt before?
qa.a: She admired Dr. Mehta and thought everything about that work was perfect, so the letdown stings more.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do next about the conference slot?
qa.a: Ask Dr. Mehta plainly why Tanmay was chosen, while keeping the way of framing questions she learned.

qa.q: Why might Amandeep ask if she will tear up her notebook?
qa.a: Amandeep may worry that Chandrika will reject everything and everyone in authority, so the question checks that she is not throwing away useful learning.

grounding: A student finds her mentor biased, keeps what he taught and refuses to distrust all authority.

passage: Thursday night. Project marks are out. Simran got 9 out of 10 for a design almost the same as mine, and I got 6. Same materials, same report length, and mine had the extra test. The professor wrote "excellent teamwork" on hers, and Simran drinks tea in the professor's cabin every Friday. I was so angry I could not eat. Then I made myself list facts: the rubric, both marks, the date I submitted. I am not going to say anything against Simran, because the marking was not her doing. Tomorrow I will email the course coordinator and ask for a recheck against the rubric. And I am still finishing my next report properly, because sulking would only cost me. 😔 Maria

qa.q: How many marks did Simran get?
qa.a: Simran got 9 out of 10.

qa.q: Why did Maria decide not to say anything against Simran?
qa.a: Maria feels the marking was not Simran's doing, so she aims her complaint at the rubric and the process.

qa.q: What did Maria plan to do, and why might it work?
qa.a: She plans to email the course coordinator for a recheck against the rubric, which rests on facts like the marks and submission date rather than on anger. 🙂

qa.q: How might Simran feel if Maria's complaint reached her?
qa.a: Simran might feel embarrassed or worried about being blamed, which is why Maria keeps the focus on the process.

grounding: A student sees grades going to a favourite and gathers facts, plans a formal request and keeps her own standards.

passage: Nikita had rehearsed the sentence on the metro all the way to campus. Professor Tanuja's door was half open, and the deadline for the exchange programme was still five weeks away, which felt safe. She knocked. "Ma'am, may I ask for a recommendation letter? I know it's a favour." She held out a folder: her résumé, the two lab reports from Professor Tanuja's course, and a short paragraph on why she wanted the programme. "I put the deadline on the first page." Tanuja flipped through it and nodded. "This makes it easy. Come back in two weeks and remind me." Nikita's shoulders dropped. She had almost told herself that professors write these letters automatically, and she was glad she hadn't.

qa.q: How many weeks were left before the exchange programme deadline?
qa.a: Five weeks were left.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she knocked, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was nervous: she rehearsed the sentence on the metro and called the request a favour, and her shoulders dropping afterwards shows relief.

qa.q: What made Nikita's request easy to say yes to?
qa.a: She asked early and politely and gave context: a résumé, two lab reports, a paragraph on her aims and the deadline. 🙂

qa.q: How might Professor Tanuja see the folder?
qa.a: Professor Tanuja probably sees that it saves effort and shows Nikita is serious, which fits the remark "This makes it easy."

grounding: A student worried about asking asks early and politely and gives context about her work.

passage: Kishore got the offer letter on a Monday, and by Tuesday afternoon he was standing at Gurleen's desk in the department office, the letter folded in his shirt pocket. Two years ago she had looked at his failing mechanics marks and asked, "What do you enjoy doing at midnight?" That question led him to data work. "Ma'am, I wouldn't be here without that chat," he said, his voice cracking a little. She waved it off, smiling. "Go and tell your juniors how you got there." On Saturday he sat in the seminar room with six second-years, an open laptop, and the same question: "What do you enjoy doing at midnight?" He wrote down their names so he could check on them in a month.

qa.q: What question did Gurleen ask Kishore two years ago?
qa.a: She asked, "What do you enjoy doing at midnight?"

qa.q: What does Kishore's cracking voice suggest about how he feels toward Gurleen?
qa.a: It suggests deep gratitude and some emotion, since her question changed his direction.

qa.q: How does Kishore pass on what he received?
qa.a: He meets six second-years on Saturday, asks them the same question and notes their names to check on them in a month.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel seeing Kishore repeat her question to juniors?
qa.a: She might feel quietly proud and glad that her guidance did not stop with him, as her smile and suggestion to tell his juniors hint. 😊

grounding: A student whose mentor changed his direction says thanks and passes on what he learned.

passage: I am Divyansh, and for most of my second year I texted my mentor Mohit sir before every decision: which elective, which internship form, even which font for my poster. He always answered, and I thought that meant I was being careful. Then he went away for a week to a conference and did not reply. I sat with three options for my project topic and felt strangely stuck, as if I had forgotten how to walk. On the fourth day I wrote a page of my own reasons for each option. When he came back I did not ask what I should do. I said, "This is what I picked and why. What am I missing?" He read it and smiled. "Now we can talk."

qa.q: How long was Mohit away at the conference?
qa.a: He was away for a week.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh feel stuck when Mohit did not reply?
qa.a: He had been checking every decision with Mohit, so he had little practice choosing for himself.

qa.q: What did Divyansh change in how he asked Mohit for advice?
qa.a: He brought his own choice and reasons and asked what he was missing, instead of asking what to do.

qa.q: How might Mohit see the earlier stream of texts?
qa.a: Mohit answered every time, but his smile at the page of reasons suggests he prefers a mentee who thinks first. 🙂

grounding: A student who waits for a mentor's instructions brings his own reasoning and grows toward independent judgement.

passage: Snow was piling against the lab window in Toronto when Noa saw the draft on the shared screen. Her name sat fourth on the paper, after Hiroshi, the senior researcher, and a student who had attended only two meetings. She had run every experiment, and for six weeks she had also covered Hiroshi's Saturday sessions with undergraduates, "as a learning chance." In the corridor she kept her voice even. "Hiroshi, I would like to talk about the author order and my Saturdays. I'm glad for what you've taught me, and I want the paper to show who did the experiments." He rubbed his neck. "I assumed you were happy to help." She suggested asking the graduate coordinator to look at the contribution list. He hesitated, then nodded. Noa walked back to her bench, her hands still shaking a little.

qa.q: Where was Noa's name on the author list?
qa.a: Her name was fourth on the paper.

qa.q: What might Noa be feeling as she speaks to Hiroshi in the corridor?
qa.a: She is nervous but determined: she keeps her voice even, and her hands are still shaking afterwards.

qa.q: Why was asking the graduate coordinator a sensible step?
qa.a: A neutral person can check the contribution list fairly, so it is not only Noa's word against Hiroshi's.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see the situation?
qa.a: His remark that he assumed she was happy to help suggests he may not have thought of it as taking her credit and time.

grounding: A guide uses a student's work and time unfairly and she politely names it, sets limits and brings in a neutral person.

passage: Counselling note, Thursday. Tarun, a second-year student, came in after the committee's notice went up on the board. He said his project guide, Anand, keeps making remarks about how he looks and, twice this month, put a hand on his back after he had stepped away. Tarun kept apologising for "making a fuss" and asked whether he had somehow encouraged it. I told him plainly that it is not his fault and that he did nothing to invite it. He had already saved the messages and written the dates in his phone. We went through how to file a written complaint with the internal committee, and I offered to sit with him when he submits it. He agreed to tell his sister tonight as well. I will check in with him on Monday.

qa.q: How many times this month did Anand put a hand on Tarun's back?
qa.a: Anand did it twice this month.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep apologising and ask whether he had encouraged it?
qa.a: He seems to fear that he caused it or is making too much of it, and the counsellor's plain reply speaks to that fear.

qa.q: What steps moved Tarun toward reporting?
qa.a: He saved the messages and dates, learned how to file a written complaint with the internal committee, and will have the counsellor beside him and tell his sister.

qa.q: What might it mean for Tarun that the counsellor offers to sit with him when he submits the complaint?
qa.a: It means he does not have to face the process alone, and a trusted adult is sharing it.

grounding: A student is affected by a guide's unwanted comments and touch; the response is recognising it as wrong, keeping records and reporting.

passage:

Pranav: I wrote the ending first, then worked backwards.
Ishita: ok I'm buying the same black notebook and copying your 6am schedule lol
Pranav: the 6am thing is only because my bus is early 😅 don't copy that
Ishita: haha fine. But the ending-first idea, that I'm keeping
Pranav: what do you want your demo to show?
Ishita: that our reminder tool is easy for my Nani to use
Pranav: then start from her taps. Ending first, but your ending
Ishita: ok. writing Nani's steps now

qa.q: What did Pranav do first when planning his demo?
qa.a: He wrote the ending first and then worked backwards.

qa.q: What does Ishita want her demo to show?
qa.a: She wants it to show that the reminder tool is easy for her Nani to use.

qa.q: Why does Pranav's question about her demo help Ishita?
qa.a: It turns his method into her own goal, so she starts from her Nani's taps instead of copying his style. 🙂

qa.q: How might Pranav feel when Ishita says she will copy his notebook and schedule?
qa.a: He seems amused and a bit concerned, which is why he explains that the 6am thing is only because of his early bus.

grounding: A junior admires a senior and learns his way of thinking rather than copying his choices.
